title: Manual handling & ergonomics
blurb: Assessing a load with TILE, lifting safely, and protecting your neck, back and wrists at the chairside.
question: A delivery of heavy boxes of gloves and a replacement oxygen cylinder arrives at reception while you're on your own, and the stock room is upstairs. You've also been getting neck and shoulder ache after long chairside sessions. What does the law expect, and how should you tackle both problems?

teach.body: Manual handling means lifting, lowering, pushing, pulling, carrying or moving a load by hand or with bodily force, and the load can be a person. Poor handling causes musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) such as back, neck and shoulder injuries. The Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 require employers to avoid hazardous manual handling so far as reasonably practicable, assess the risk of any that can't be avoided, and reduce that risk. You must follow the safe systems and use the aids provided.

teach.body: Dental nurses spend hours in fixed, forward-leaning postures, which strains the neck, shoulders, back and wrists. Most chairside aches come from craning to see, twisting to reach the tray, and holding the arms raised. The fix is to set up before you start: adjust your stool, position the patient chair, keep instruments within easy reach, and move your stool rather than twisting your body. Take short breaks to stretch between patients.

rows.label: Back
values: Move the stool, face the task

rows.label: Feet
values: Flat on the floor or foot ring

teach.caption: The nurse is usually seated a little higher than the operator, to see into the mouth without leaning.

teach.body: Staff who use computers for long periods are covered by the Health and Safety (Display Screen Equipment) Regulations 1992. The employer must assess the workstation, plan breaks or changes of activity, and arrange eye tests on request. Setting the screen at eye level, the chair at the right height and the keyboard close reduces neck, back and wrist strain.

teach.text: Bending your knees isn't enough on its own. The classic cause of back injury is TWISTING while holding a load. Turn with your feet. And waiting for a 'stronger colleague' is not a control: assess the load and use help or handling aids.

items: Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992: avoid, assess, reduce.
Safe lift: plan, stable base, bend knees, load close, no twisting.
Never lift patients; use aids and follow training.
Chairside: adjust stool and chair, keep items in reach, move rather than twist, take breaks.
Report persistent aches early so your workstation and technique can be reviewed.

summary: You can now explain the legal duties around manual handling, assess a load using TILE, describe a safe lift, choose safer approaches for dental handling tasks, and set up your chairside position to protect your neck, back and wrists.

A.q: A delivery of heavy boxes arrives at reception. Which action best supports safe manual handling?
options: Carry several boxes at once to save time
Wait for the strongest colleague to do it
Lift quickly so the strain lasts a shorter time
Assess the load; use help or aids if needed
A.why: Assess the load first (TILE), then reduce the risk by splitting it, getting help or using a trolley.

whyNot.0: Carrying several boxes increases weight and blocks your view.
whyNot.1: Relying on one person's strength isn't a safe system; assess and use aids.
whyNot.2: Jerky, rushed lifts increase the risk of injury.

A.q: In the TILE assessment, what does the 'E' stand for?
options: Effort
Equipment
Environment
Ergonomics
A.why: TILE stands for Task, Individual, Load and Environment.

whyNot.0: Effort is considered under Task and Load, but it isn't the E.
whyNot.1: Handling aids may be part of the solution, but the E is Environment.
whyNot.3: Ergonomics is the wider science, not a TILE letter.

A.q: A nurse regularly gets neck and shoulder pain after long chairside sessions. Which action best addresses the cause?
options: Take painkillers before each session
Review posture, seating and chair position
Use a heat pack on the neck at the end of the day
Accept it as part of the job
A.why: Chairside aches usually come from posture and set-up. Fixing those removes the cause.

whyNot.0: Painkillers mask symptoms and leave the cause in place.
whyNot.2: Heat may ease pain, but it doesn't fix the posture causing it.
whyNot.3: MSDs are preventable; they shouldn't be accepted.

B.q: A colleague lifts a heavy box of stock while twisting quickly to put it on a shelf. What is the main risk?
options: Damage to the stock in the box
Straining the eyes while turning quickly
Dropping the box on the floor
Musculoskeletal injury to the back
B.why: Twisting while holding a load is a major cause of back injury.

whyNot.0: Stock damage is possible, but the main concern is injury.
whyNot.1: Eye strain is unrelated to lifting.
whyNot.2: Dropping the box is a risk, but the twisting lift itself is the main hazard.

B.q: Which law requires employers to avoid, assess and reduce hazardous manual handling?
options: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992
The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998
The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002
The Display Screen Equipment Regulations 1992
B.why: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 set the avoid, assess, reduce approach.

whyNot.3: The DSE Regulations cover computer workstations.

B.q: When lifting a box from the floor, where should the load be held?
options: At arm's length to protect your clothes
Close to your waist
Above your shoulders
On one hip, to free a hand
B.why: Keeping the load close to the waist reduces the strain on your back.

whyNot.0: Holding a load at arm's length greatly increases strain on the back.
whyNot.2: Lifting above the shoulders is a high-risk posture.
whyNot.3: Carrying on one side loads the spine unevenly.

C.q: A replacement oxygen cylinder needs to go from reception to the surgery. What is the safest approach?
options: Roll it carefully along the floor on its side
Carry it over your shoulder
Use a cylinder trolley, kept upright
Drag it by the valve
C.why: A cylinder trolley reduces the handling risk and keeps the cylinder upright and secure.

whyNot.0: Rolling a cylinder risks damage to the valve and loss of control.
whyNot.1: Carrying a cylinder on the shoulder is a serious manual handling risk.
whyNot.3: Dragging by the valve can damage it and cause a dangerous gas release.

C.q: Which of these is part of the 'Individual' in a TILE assessment?
options: Whether the floor is slippery
Whether the load is hard to grip
Whether the person is pregnant
Whether the route includes stairs
C.why: The Individual covers the person's capability: health, strength, training, pregnancy or existing injury.

whyNot.0: A slippery floor is part of the Environment.
whyNot.1: Grip is part of the Load.
whyNot.3: Stairs are part of the Environment.

C.q: At the chairside you keep twisting to reach the bracket table. What is the best change?
options: Reposition the tray or your stool
Twist faster to save time
Stand for the whole procedure
Ask the patient to turn towards you
C.why: Bring the work within easy reach, or move your stool, so you face the task without twisting.

whyNot.2: Standing all session can cause its own strain and may reduce access.
whyNot.3: Moving the patient may compromise the operator's access and isn't the fix.

reteach.title: Pack the car before the trip
reteach.question: Before a long car journey you check the route, the weather, the passengers and the luggage. How is that like planning a lift?

blocks.body: TILE is your pre-trip check. Task: how far, how many trips, any awkward turns? Individual: are you fit to drive (lift) today? Load: how heavy is the luggage, will it shift? Environment: is the road icy, narrow or dark? You wouldn't set off without checking, and you shouldn't lift without it either. If something isn't right, change the plan: lighter loads, a trolley, or a second person.

explain.body: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992: employers must avoid hazardous manual handling where reasonably practicable, assess what can't be avoided, and reduce the risk. Employees follow the safe system and use the aids provided.

test.q: What is the FIRST thing the regulations ask employers to consider?
options: Training staff to lift correctly
Avoiding hazardous handling altogether
Providing back support belts for all staff
Recording all lifts in a log
test.why: The first step is to avoid hazardous manual handling where reasonably practicable, for example by having deliveries taken straight to the stock room.

whyNot.0: Training helps reduce risk but comes after avoiding and assessing.
whyNot.2: Back belts are not a recognised primary control.
whyNot.3: Logging lifts isn't a requirement of the regulations.

explain.body: Task, Individual, Load, Environment. Each letter is a set of questions about what could make the lift risky.

test.q: A box has no handles and its contents shift as you move it. Which part of TILE does this relate to?
options: Task
Individual
Load
Environment
test.why: An unstable load that is hard to grip is a Load factor.

whyNot.0: Task is about the movements involved, such as twisting or distance.
whyNot.1: Individual is about the person's capability.
whyNot.3: Environment is about the surroundings, such as floors and stairs.

explain.body: Plan, take a stable base, bend the knees with a natural back curve, grip firmly with the load close, lift smoothly without twisting, put down then adjust.

test.q: Which is the safest way to change direction while carrying a box?
options: Twist from the waist
Swing the box to build momentum
Hold the box higher and turn
Step round with your feet
test.why: Moving the feet keeps the spine aligned and avoids twisting under load.

whyNot.0: Twisting under load is a major cause of back injury.
whyNot.1: Swinging makes the load harder to control.

explain.body: Set your stool so you sit back supported with feet flat, sit slightly higher than the operator, keep instruments within reach, move your stool rather than twisting, and stretch between patients. Report persistent pain early.

items: Adjust stool height and back support

test.q: Why is the dental nurse usually seated slightly higher than the operator?
options: To see into the mouth without leaning
To stay out of the aerosol
To reach the overhead light
To keep a safer distance from the patient
test.why: A slightly higher position gives a clear view of the working area without craning the neck.

whyNot.1: Height doesn't take you out of the aerosol; PPE and suction do that.
whyNot.2: The operator usually adjusts the light.
whyNot.3: Distance from the patient isn't the purpose.
